notes:
Here is the verse-by-verse commentary on Numbers 21, compiled from the available sources:

---

## Numbers 21 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — The Canaanite King of Arad Attacks

- **The identity of Arad**: The phrase is better read "the Canaanite, the king of Arad," with Arad being a place rather than a person's name (cf. Joshua 12:14; Judges 1:16). It was situated in the Negev (the "South"), about 17 miles south of Hebron at modern Tel Arad. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **"By the way of Atharim"**: The KJV renders this "the way of the spies." The Hebrew word *atharim* is uncertain — it may be a proper place name (so the Septuagint), or it could be an unusual plural related to "spies" (so the Targums). If it means "spies," the reference is to the route the twelve spies took 38 years earlier into Canaan (Numbers 13:17, 22). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **The victory and loss**: Israel lost some men taken captive, indicating they were caught off-guard. This defeat prompted them to turn to the Lord. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Chronological questions**: Commentators note that this battle is hard to place chronologically — Israel was not yet in the Negev during their wanderings. The Pulpit Commentary discusses several theories: the narrative may be displaced and actually belong to an earlier time, or Israel may have sent raiding parties from their camp at Mount Hor. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **The Lutheran reading**: 1517.org treats this opening victory as part of God's pattern of grace — even after Israel's failures, God continues to give them victories that foreshadow the greater conquest to come. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-numbers-214-9-lent-4-series-b)

### v. 2 — Israel's Vow of *Herem* (Devotion to Destruction)

- **The vow explained**: Israel vowed that if God gave them victory, they would "utterly destroy" (Hebrew *charam*; LXX *anathematizo*) the cities — meaning they would devote everything to God, taking no spoil for themselves. This was not bloodlust but a setting aside of the spoils exclusively for the Lord. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-21-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **Spurgeon's note**: Charles Spurgeon observed that Israel "did not depend upon their own prowess in war … they went at once to the Lord, and spread their case before him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Moral character of *herem***: The Pulpit Commentary defends the practice by placing it in its historical context — just as modern soldiers are instruments of their nation's policy, the Israelite soldier was an instrument of God's judgment on a morally depraved civilization. The vow removed the battle from the sphere of private revenge or greed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 3 — Victory and the Naming of Hormah

- **"Hormah"** means "devoted to destruction," from the same Hebrew root *charam*. This is the second time this name appears: Israel had previously been defeated as far as Hormah when they tried to enter Canaan in unbelief (Numbers 14:45). Now, God brought them back to the same location and gave them a victory that reversed the earlier defeat. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-21-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Did the destruction happen immediately?** Ellicott notes it is unclear whether the vow was fulfilled at once or later. The cities of Arad still appear in Joshua 12:14 and Judges 1:16-17, suggesting the full conquest came later under Joshua. Gill suggests the vow was made now but executed in Joshua's time. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **Typological significance**: Pastor David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes this was "the beginning of Israel's wars of conquest and God's judgment against the Canaanites." It gave the new generation a foretaste of what God would do. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

---

### vv. 4-9 — The Bronze Serpent (The Central Passage of the Chapter)

### v. 4 — Discouragement on the Journey

- **"To go around the land of Edom"**: After Edom refused passage (Numbers 20:14-21), Israel had to turn south toward the Red Sea (the Arabah valley toward the Gulf of Aqaba) and then march north around Edom on its eastern side. This meant going away from Canaan — a physically and emotionally discouraging detour. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **"The soul of the people became very discouraged"**: Literally, their soul "was shortened" or "straitened" — they became impatient, short of breath, fretful. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Arabah is a stony, barren plain subject to sand-storms, and the season was likely one of the hottest (the sixth month of the 40th year). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **The Homiletics section** of the Pulpit Commentary draws applications for the Christian pilgrim: discouragements may arise from the *direction* of the way (apparently retreating from God's goal), the *length* of the way (longer because God avoids a war-path), the *roughness* of the way, and the *companionships* of complainers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 5 — Speaking Against God and Moses

- **"The people spoke against God and against Moses"**: This is the first time in all the wilderness complaints that the people are said to speak *directly against God*. In eight previous passages they spoke against Moses (Exodus 15:24, 16:2, 17:3; Numbers 12:1, 14:2, 16:3, 16:41, 20:2), but now their boldness in sin escalated. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **"We detest this wretched (light) bread"**: Gill explains the Hebrew doubling of the root intensifies the contempt — they called the manna "exceedingly vile, mean, and despicable." The Pulpit Commentary compares it to their fathers' complaint in Numbers 11:6 — they saw the manna as unsavory and unsubstantial compared to heavy Egyptian food. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **Spurgeon's observation**: "When the grumbling humour is on us we complain of anything and everything … nothing is right: nothing can be right." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **A Lutheran perspective**: 1517.org notes that this final complaint "culminates the entire series" because for the first time the people spoke against God directly — yet the account "continues to hold forth God's grace for salvation." (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-numbers-214-9-lent-4-series-b)

### v. 6 — The LORD Sends "Fiery Serpents"

- **"Fiery serpents"** (*nechashim seraphim*): The word *saraph* means "burning one." The Pulpit Commentary argues from comparison with Isaiah's seraphim (Isaiah 6:2, 6) and Ezekiel's visions (Ezekiel 1:7) that the name refers to the fiery-red or burnished, coppery colour of these snakes, not simply the burning sensation of the bite. Moses later made a bronze (copper) serpent to match their appearance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **Natural candidates**: Travelers report several venomous snakes still in the Arabah region — horned vipers, puff-adders, and especially the "carpet viper" (*Echis carinatus*). Gill cites ancient sources (Diodorus Siculus, Herodotus) describing Arabian flying serpents of red or scarlet colour whose bite is incurable and brings quick death. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **The connection with their sin**: Enduring Word draws the parallels: they despised bread from heaven → God gave them serpents from the earth; they despised God's blessing → God gave them burning poison; they despised the life God sustained → God gave them death. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **The generation affected**: Guzik suggests the victims were probably mostly the older generation of unbelief — God's final fulfilment of His promise that they would perish in the wilderness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Lutheran distinctive**: 1517.org identifies the serpents' poison as a picture of "original sin (Genesis 3) since the fall." The serpent that brought death in Eden now brings death in the wilderness, but through the same image — a serpent on a pole — comes healing. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-numbers-214-9-lent-4-series-b)

### v. 7 — Confession and Intercession

- **"We have sinned"**: This is the first time in the book of Numbers that the people unambiguously confess their sin. Gill notes that they acknowledged speaking "against the LORD, and against thee" — both dimensions of their sin. Enduring Word highlights that the new generation, though capable of deeper sin, also had "hearts softer and quicker to repent." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **"Pray to the LORD that He take away the serpents"**: The Pulpit Commentary notes this is the first (and only recorded) time the people directly asked for Moses' intercession — although Pharaoh had done so several times. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **Moses' response**: Despite having been spoken against, Moses immediately intercedes, demonstrating the meekness for which he was known (Numbers 12:3). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 8 — God's Unusual Prescription: "Look and Live"

- **"Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole"**: The word for pole is *nes*, meaning a standard, banner, or ensign. The Septuagint uses *sēmeion* (sign). This was to be raised high so all the camp could see it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html)
- **The "foolishness" of the remedy**: Enduring Word emphasises there was no logical connection between looking at a bronze serpent and being healed — God deliberately chose something that seemed foolish so that trust would be purely in His word. This principle is echoed in 1 Corinthians 1:18-25. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Lutheran typology (three points from Luther)**: Martin Luther, in a sermon on John 3, identified three aspects of the type: (1) The serpent was of brass/copper, reddish like the burning victims, yet without poison — as Christ took the form of sinful flesh yet was without sin (Romans 8:3; 2 Corinthians 5:21). (2) It was lifted up on a pole as a public sign — as Christ was lifted up on the cross, a public triumph over evil powers (Colossians 2:14-15). (3) Healing came by looking — as we look in faith to Christ crucified. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/numbers-21.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/numbers-21.html)
- **Baptist perspective (Spurgeon)**: Spurgeon preached an entire sermon on this passage ("The Mysteries of the Brazen Serpent") emphasising that like the brazen serpent, Christ is despised — some said "it was a serpent that did the mischief; how can a serpent undo it?" just as people ask, "It was by man that sin came; can a man be the means of salvation?" (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-mysteries-of-the-brazen-serpent)
- **Reformed/Baptist perspective (John MacArthur/GTY)**: The incident is described as "an illustration of justification by faith" — the point Jesus was making to Nicodemus in John 3. (https://www.gty.org/blogs/B181219/the-gospel-distilled)

### v. 9 — The Bronze Serpent Made and Looked Upon

- **"A serpent of brass"**: The Hebrew is *nechash nechoshet* — a play on words ("a bronze serpent"). Gill notes that copper/brass was the fitting metal because its reddish colour resembled the "fiery" serpents. Copper was available from nearby Punon (Numbers 33:42), a place famous for brass mines. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **Jesus' own interpretation**: John 3:14-15 — "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life." Ellicott elaborates: Christ became "sin for us" (2 Corinthians 5:21) just as the bronze serpent represented the judged and defeated thing that had been killing the people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html)
- **"When he looked … he lived"**: Enduring Word stresses the simplicity — no works, no priest, no ceremony, no touching required. "If any life still remained in the poisoned person, they could look and live. Some who had been just bitten looked and lived; some who were almost dead looked and lived." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Spurgeon's conversion**: Charles Spurgeon came to Christ after hearing a sermon on Isaiah 45:22 ("Look unto Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth") connected to this account. He later adopted an engraving of Moses lifting up the serpent as his ministry logo. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Hezekiah's reform**: The bronze serpent was preserved for centuries, but by Hezekiah's time it had become an idol called *Nehushtan* and the king broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Hezekiah "estimated the symbol of salvation at its true value, as being in itself worthless, and under certain circumstances mischievous." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **The Lutheran emphasis**: 1517.org calls it a "caduceus of sorts" — an image drawing attention to "the spiritual first responder for sin." Jesus, hung on a cursed tree for our sins, is the one to whom we look and receive healing and eternal life. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-numbers-214-9-lent-4-series-b)
- **Archaeological note**: At Timna (about 15 miles north of Eilat), a Midianite tent-shrine from around 1150 BC contained a copper snake 5 inches long, providing remarkable confirmation of serpent imagery in the wilderness period. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

---

### vv. 10-20 — The Journey Toward Moab

### v. 10 — Oboth

- The name Oboth may mean "bottles" or "waterskins." Gill suggests this may be where they obtained water and filled their containers. In the station list of Numbers 33, two other camps (Zalmonah and Punon) intervene between Mount Hor and Oboth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 11 — Iye-abarim

- "Iye" means "ruins" or "heaps"; "Abarim" means "ridges" or "ranges." The site lay east of Moab in the wilderness. Israel was marching northward along the eastern side of the Edomite and Moabite territories. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 12 — The Valley (Brook) of Zered

- The Zered is likely the modern Wadi Kerek, flowing westward into the Dead Sea. This crossing marked a significant transition, as Deuteronomy 2:13-14 notes that the entire generation of warriors had now perished by the time they crossed the Zered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 13 — The Arnon River

- The Arnon (modern Wadi Mujib in Jordan) was the border between Moab and the Amorites. Israel camped on its northern side, now entering territory claimed by the Amorites (who had taken it from Moab — see v. 26). They crossed it in the upper desert reaches, not the deep gorge near the Dead Sea. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

### vv. 14-15 — The Book of the Wars of the LORD

- **What was this book?** Nothing is known of it beyond these two verses. The Pulpit Commentary suggests it was an ancient collection of victory songs and war odes, perhaps compiled from the spontaneous poetic effusions of Israel's emerging national life. Its archaic language testifies to its authenticity. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **The quotation**: The Hebrew of verse 14 is very difficult. The Pulpit Commentary renders it "Vaheb in whirlwind, and the brooks of Arnon" rather than the KJV's "What he did in the Red Sea." *Vaheb* is probably an unknown place name, and *Suphah* may be a location rather than "Red Sea." The point of the quotation, however, is clear: it confirms the Amorite conquest of territory north of the Arnon that had formerly belonged to Moab. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **Gill's reading**: The "Book of the Wars of the LORD" was a history of wars from the time of Abraham onward, and the quotation in v. 14 refers to what Sihon (or the LORD through him) did to the Moabites — destroying "Vaheb in Suphah" and taking the brooks of the Arnon. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)
- **Apologetic note (Enduring Word)**: The mere mention of a lost book does not mean the Bible is incomplete. Paul quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28), and neither those poets' full works belong in Scripture. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

### vv. 16-18 — The Song of the Well at Beer

- **"Beer"** means "well." Unlike previous water crises where the people complained, here God proactively promised water. He told Moses to gather the people, and the leaders dug with their staffs. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **The song (v. 17-18)**: "Spring up, O well! Sing to it!" This is the first time Israel is recorded singing since the Song of the Sea at the Red Sea (Exodus 15) — about 40 years earlier. The joyful tone signals a new season of trust and praise. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **"The nobles dug … with their scepters and staffs"**: Spurgeon preached on this detail: "They digged with their staves — not very first-class tools. Would not the mattock and the spade have been better? Ay, but they did as they were told." He applied it: "We must dig as we can. We must use what abilities we have." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **"By the direction of the lawgiver"** (*mechokek*): This could mean Moses himself directed the work, or more literally "with the scepter" — the leaders dug with the very rods that were emblems of their authority. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)

### vv. 18b-20 — Mattanah, Nahaliel, Bamoth, Pisgah

- These stations mark Israel's march northward through territory east of the Jordan. Mattanah means "gift"; Nahaliel means "torrent of God"; Bamoth means "high places." The final stop is the valley in Moab "where the top of Pisgah overlooks the wasteland" — the same Pisgah (Mount Nebo) from which Moses would later view the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 34:1). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

---

### vv. 21-35 — Victories over Sihon and Og

### vv. 21-22 — Israel's Peaceful Request to Sihon

- **"Let us pass through your land"**: The request mirrors the one made to Edom (Numbers 20:17). Israel promised to stay on the King's Highway, not to turn into fields or vineyards, and not to drink from wells without paying. Deuteronomy 2:26-29 adds that they also offered to pay for any water they consumed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)

### v. 23 — Sihon Refuses and Attacks

- Unlike the Edomites who merely threatened and blocked passage, Sihon gathered his entire army and attacked Israel at Jahaz. Enduring Word notes that God hardened Sihon's heart (Deuteronomy 2:30) as part of His plan to give Israel practice victories before facing the larger challenges of Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

### vv. 24-26 — Israel Defeats Sihon and Takes His Land

- **"From the Arnon to the Jabbok"**: This was approximately 50 miles of territory east of the Jordan River, between two major gorges. Israel stopped at the Ammonite border because it was fortified, and also because God had forbidden them to take Ammonite land (Deuteronomy 2:19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html)
- **Background on Heshbon (v. 26)**: Sihon had himself conquered this territory from a previous Moabite king, taking everything as far south as the Arnon. So Israel was not taking land that belonged to Moab (whom God had told them not to dispossess), but land the Amorites had previously seized from Moab. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/21.htm)

### vv. 27-30 — The Taunt Song (The "Poets' Song")

- **An Amorite victory song, now turned against them**: These verses are an ancient poetic fragment, originally celebrating Sihon's conquest of Moab (vv. 27-29), then adapted with an Israelite conclusion celebrating Sihon's overthrow (v. 30). The Pulpit Commentary renders them as a quotation the Israelites used to taunt the defeated Amorites. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)
- **"Chemosh"** (v. 29): The national god of Moab. The song mocks Chemosh for being unable to protect his people — his sons became refugees and his daughters captives. This is a polemic against the impotence of pagan deities. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- Ellicott's rendering of the song shifts dramatically at v. 30: "We cast them down; Heshbon is perished even unto Dibon … which reacheth unto Medeba." This final stanza is the Israelite boast over their defeated enemy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html)

### v. 31 — Israel Dwells in Amorite Land

- Ellicott notes the Hebrew verb here likely means "sojourned" or "abode" in the sense of a temporary encampment — the permanent settlement east of the Jordan came only after Moses' death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-21.html)

### v. 32 — The Capture of Jazer

- Moses sent spies to Jazer (a city in the Amorite region north of Heshbon), and Israel captured its surrounding villages, driving out the remaining Amorites. The Pulpit Commentary notes this as part of the systematic conquest of the Amorite holdings. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/21.htm)

### vv. 33-35 — The Defeat of Og, King of Bashan

- **Og of Bashan**: Og was a giant king (Deuteronomy 3:11 notes his iron bedstead was about 13.5 feet long). Bashan was the fertile highland region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its rich pastures and strong cities. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **"Do not fear him"**: God directly reassured Moses, promising Og and all his people into Israel's hands, just as He had done with Sihon. The defeat was total — Og, his sons, and his entire army were struck down "until no remnant was left." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)
- **Significance**: Enduring Word notes that these victories gave Israel possession of the entire Transjordan — the land that would eventually be allotted to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. These were "practice victories" that built the new generation's confidence before crossing the Jordan into Canaan proper. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-21/)

## Summary of the Chapter's Structure

The Precept Austin commentary structures Numbers 21 in four movements:
1. **vv. 1-3** — Israel Victorious over Arad (the first conquest under the new generation)
2. **vv. 4-9** — Deadly Serpents, Divine Solution (the bronze serpent, the typological heart of the chapter)
3. **vv. 10-20** — Israel Approaches Moab (journey stations, water at Beer, joyful singing)
4. **vv. 21-35** — Victory over Sihon and Og (conquest of the Transjordan Amorite kingdoms)

(https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-21-commentary)

Irving Jensen (as cited in Precept Austin) summarises: "When God promised to give the land of Canaan to His people, He did not say that this land of rest and plenty would come to them without battle or trial. There would be battles, but He would give victory." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-21-commentary)

## Where the Traditions Differ or Converge

- **On the bronze serpent as type of Christ**: All Protestant traditions consulted (Reformed/Baptist via Enduring Word and GTY; Lutheran via 1517.org and Luther's sermons; Spurgeon representing Baptist) are in substantial agreement: the lifted serpent prefigures Christ crucified, who became sin for us so that looking to Him in faith brings eternal life. The Lutheran sources particularly emphasise the link to original sin and the "poison" of the fall.

- **On the *herem* (devotion to destruction)**: The Pulpit Commentary (older Anglican) provides the most extended moral defence, placing it within the framework of divine judgment on a depraved civilisation. Enduring Word (broadly Reformed/Baptist charismatic) similarly treats it as part of God's unique judgment-war against the Canaanites. No denominational disagreement was found among the sources consulted.

- **On the "Book of the Wars of the LORD"**: Gill (Baptist/Reformed) and the Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) agree it was a lost ancient collection of victory songs. Gill speculates it covered wars from Abraham's time; the Pulpit Commentary sees it as a contemporary collection of Israel's wilderness odes.
